**Video:** [Lec 07 — IID Assumption](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C83xmx80tMo)

### Learning goals
- Unpack **i.i.d.**: identically distributed + statistically independent
- See two equivalent views of a dataset of size $n$
- Distinguish independence **across samples** vs across **dimensions**
- State the course definition of ML: given $\mathcal{D}$, estimate $P$ (or conditionals / marginals)

### Before this clicks
Dataset from Lecture 6:

$$
\mathcal{D}=\bigl\{(x_i,y_i)\bigr\}_{i=1}^{n}
\quad\text{“sampled i.i.d. from”}\quad
P_{X,Y}.
$$

Events $A,B$ are independent if $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. For RVs, independence means the joint factors into a product of marginals.

---

## 1. Identically distributed

Think of the $n$ pairs as coming from $n$ random variables (each vector-valued), all with the **same** law $P_{X,Y}$.

Equivalently: the experimental conditions do not change across the $n$ draws (same hospital protocol, same population story, … — intuition only; the math is “same distribution”).

If you train on lung X-rays and test on brain MRI **without** rebuilding the model story, the identical-distribution assumption is broken.

---

## 2. Independent (statistical sense)

Events $A,B$ independent $\Leftrightarrow$ $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.

For RVs: joint = product of marginals. For the dataset viewed as $n$ RVs $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ (each $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$),

$$
P_{Z_1,\ldots,Z_n} = P_{Z_1}\cdots P_{Z_n}
$$

when they are independent (and with identical laws, each factor equals the same $P_Z$).

---

## 3. Two viewpoints of the same dataset

| View | Story | Need the words “i.i.d.”? |
|------|-------|---------------------------|
| A | $n$ **realizations** of **one** RV $Z$ | “i.i.d.” is almost redundant — one law, many trials |
| B | **One** realization of **$n$** RVs $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ | Yes: identical laws + mutual independence |

Textbooks write $\mathcal{D}\sim P$ with a tilde for “sampled from.” **Sampling** means repeating the underlying random experiment.

---

## 4. Critical: independence across *points*, not *pixels*

**IID does *not* say** that the $D$ coordinates inside one vector $x_i$ are independent.

- Image 1 independent of image 2: **yes** (the usual IID claim).
- Pixel $(1,1)$ independent of pixel $(1,2)$ inside the same image: **not** assumed in general (nearby pixels are dependent).

Some algorithms *add* a stronger assumption of independence across dimensions; that is a separate modeling choice.

---

## 5. What breaks when IID breaks?

Algorithms we build will **use** independence and identical laws in their math. If test points come from a different experiment / different law, those algorithms are not entitled to work.

Whether faces and buildings are “one experiment” or two is a **design choice**. Merge them into one giant dataset and you can call them one law; train on faces only and test on buildings and you violated the identical-distribution story you baked into training.

---

## 6. Supervised / unsupervised / self-supervised (nomenclature)

Class view: everything is estimating laws of RVs on $\Omega$.

| Name people use | Rough meaning |
|-----------------|---------------|
| Supervised | Some coordinates called “labels” $Y$ exist |
| Unsupervised | Only $X$; no separate $Y$ |
| Self-supervised | Mask / split some dimensions of $X$ and treat them as a fake $Y$ (e.g. inpainting) |

Labels often come from human judgment; that is why supervised data is expensive — not because the math is different.

---

## 7. Formal problem statement of ML (this course)

$$
\text{Given }\mathcal{D}\text{ sampled from unknown }P,\quad
\text{estimate }P\text{ (or conditionals / marginals)}.
$$

Often write $P_{X}$ and allow $Y$ to be folded into $X$.

- Estimating $P(Y\mid X)$ with discrete $Y$: classification  
- Estimating $P(Y\mid X)$ with continuous $Y$: regression  
- Estimating joints / marginals and learning to **sample**: generative modeling  

**Discriminative** methods in this course mostly estimate useful conditionals without insisting on a full generative sampler.

> Slogan from class: *All machine learning is: given $\mathcal{D}$, estimate $P$.*

---

## 8. Tiny concrete example

Three coin tosses recorded as $1=$heads, $0=$tails: $(1,0,1)$.

- **IID view B:** three Bernoulli RVs, same $p$, independent, so

$$
P(1,0,1)=p\cdot(1-p)\cdot p.
$$

- **Not claimed:** nothing about “coordinates of a vector image” here — each toss is already a full data point.

If the coin secretly changes after toss 2, identical distribution fails and that product formula is the wrong model.

---

## 9. Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|----------------|
| IID = pixels independent | No — samples independent. |
| “Independent” in English | Means the product rule for joints / events. |
| Train and test can be any domains | Test should match the law you estimated under. |
| Supervised ≠ unsupervised mathematically | Same distribution-estimation game; different which coordinates you name. |
